abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene. Although the mutant huntingtin protein is expressed from conception, clinical symptoms typically emerge in mid-adulthood. Imaging and molecular studies have raised the possibility that HD may involve neurodevelopmental abnormalities, but direct evidence at the single-cell level in the human fetal brain has been lacking. Here we investigated whether early, cell type-specific transcriptional vulnerabilities arise during neurodevelopment, persist into adult pathology, and might be rescued. To address this, we performed single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the lateral ganglionic eminence (LGE) and cortex from a rare, anatomically intact human HD fetal brain, alongside matched controls. These data were complemented by an allelic series of HD mouse embryos and cross-compared with already published human post-mortem brains and brain organoid models' datasets. Neural progenitors displayed the highest number of differentially expressed genes in the human fetal brain, and were also impacted in the HD mouse model, where additional cell types displayed transcriptional alterations. Notably, human HD progenitor transcriptional signatures were moderately enriched in the developing mouse LGE. These progenitors exhibited increased expression of synaptic pathways coupled with reduced expression of cell maintenance genes. Cross-comparison with publicly available post-mortem HD datasets revealed that components of this transcriptional signature persist into adulthood. Furthermore, cellular interactions were found to mitigate these alterations, highlighting a potentially rescuable fetal-to-adult transcriptional signature with important implications for HD pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies. Together, these findings reinforce the view of HD as a disorder with developmental origins, in which early transcriptional changes may shape neuronal function while increasing susceptibility to later neurodegeneration.

abstract: TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

abstract: Immune checkpoint blockade has transformed cancer therapy, but immune-related adverse events (irAEs) remain a major, sometimes fatal, limitation, and the lack of robust preclinical models has hindered mechanistic insight. We present the lifestyle-induced susceptibility to irAEs (LISA) model, in which diet-driven metabolic and microbial alterations recreate human-like susceptibility to anti-PD-1 toxicity. LISA recapitulates multi-organ irAEs with immune infiltration and cytokine production, severity depending on sex, age, treatment modality, and immunotherapy response. Mechanistically, dysbiosis marked by Akkermansia muciniphila enrichment accompanies aberrant immune activation, driving regulatory T cell (Treg) fragility and CD8+ cytotoxic effector populations, both observed in patients with irColitis. Dietary reversal, metabolite supplementation, and blocking interferon (IFN)-γ production or signaling in Tregs restored Treg stability and resolved inflammation. Human-to-mouse fecal microbiome transfer interacts with recipient diet to shape susceptibility. Together, these findings identify dietary, microbial, and immune drivers of irAEs, which can be leveraged to improve immunotherapy responses while minimizing toxicity.

abstract: Metabolites are increasingly recognized as circulating molecules that regulate physiology, yet the mechanisms that couple local intracellular production to organism-wide action remain poorly defined. Using the anorexigenic metabolite N-lactoyl-phenylalanine (Lac-Phe) as a model system, we identify the orphan transporter MCT6/SLC16A5 as a physiologic intestinal Lac-Phe exporter. This mechanism controls the extent to which intracellularly synthesized Lac-Phe acquires systemic activity. MCT6 transports Lac-Phe in vitro, mediates Lac-Phe efflux in cells, and is required for maintaining normal circulating Lac-Phe levels in vivo, particularly following metformin treatment or high-intensity exercise. High-fat-diet-fed mice with global or intestinal epithelial-specific deletion of MCT6 exhibit resistance to metformin-associated weight loss. Bypassing the transport defect with exogenous Lac-Phe normalizes the body weight phenotype of MCT6-knockout (KO) mice. These data connect MCT6 to Lac-Phe and gut glycolytic flux and underscore the importance of transporter-mediated release in the conversion of an intracellular metabolic state into a circulating metabolite effector.

abstract: DNA's anti-parallel structure presents a topological challenge to the replisome, as leading and lagging strands must be synthesized in opposite directions. How lagging-strand synthesis is coordinated with leading-strand synthesis remains unresolved in eukaryotes. To address this question, we directly visualized the dynamics of lagging-strand polymerases Pol α and Pol δ at active replication forks using single-molecule imaging in Xenopus nuclear extracts. Surprisingly, we find that neither Pol α nor Pol δ is stably tethered to the replisome. Instead, lagging-strand synthesis occurs distributively and entails the rapid recruitment of new molecules of Pol α and Pol δ for each Okazaki fragment. Consequently, leading- and lagging-strand synthesis are not intrinsically coupled. We propose that metazoans solve the problem of anti-parallel replication not by actively coordinating leading- and lagging-strand synthesis, but instead simply by recruiting new polymerases to synthesize each Okazaki fragment.

abstract: Dysregulated mRNA translation is a critical driver of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) progression. While translation initiation is extensively studied, mechanisms governing translation elongation in AML remain unclear. Here, we show that the RNA methyltransferase ALKBH8 is overexpressed in patients with AML and correlates with poor prognosis. ALKBH8 is required for the proliferation and leukemogenic capacity of human and murine AML cells in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, ALKBH8 promotes translation-coupled mRNA stabilization via its methyltransferase domain. Loss of ALKBH8 induces ribosome pausing and preferentially destabilizes transcripts enriched in adenine-ending codons. Specifically, ALKBH8 regulates the expression of the DNA repair gene BRCA1 in a codon-dependent manner, supporting homologous recombination and cell survival. Moreover, ALKBH8 depletion sensitizes AML cells to the PARP inhibitor olaparib. Collectively, our study reveals a codon-specific mechanism of ALKBH8-mediated translation, highlighting the ALKBH8-BRCA1 axis as a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

abstract: Lenvatinib is a first-line therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Emerging studies suggest resistance evolves through dynamic multi-step processes. Here, using multi-timepoint and multi-omics sampling, we characterized the trajectory of lenvatinib resistance in HCC cells and identified three adaptive states marked by state transitions. Multi-omics analyses and functional validation identified amphiregulin (AREG) as a key transient mediator of resistance in our models. AREG is a sufficient and dominant ligand to promote cell survival through epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) activation. Pharmacological inhibition of the AREG-EGFR axis specifically targeted early-resistant cells. Furthermore, AREG upregulation was validated in additional replicate experiments and another HCC cell line. Mechanistically, a focal deletion on chromosome 3p may contribute to NF-κB activation and AREG expression. This study delineates a recurrent yet transient adaptive mechanism and suggests new therapeutic opportunities-such as combination therapies targeting transient resistance mechanisms-to prevent or overcome drug resistance.

abstract: Dopamine regulates the frequency of motor actions, but it is unclear whether it similarly regulates the duration of discrete behaviors. Here, we show that dopamine signaling within the medial accumbens shell reinforces actions while simultaneously constraining their duration. When mice hold down a lever to continuously self-stimulate dopamine axons in the medial accumbens shell, hold-downs are rarely longer than 5 s, and higher stimulation frequencies elicit shorter, but more numerous, lever hold-downs. This disengaging property of medial accumbens shell dopamine also applies to consummatory behavior, as mice are quicker to both terminate and reinitiate bouts of licking paired with high-frequency dopamine axon stimulation. Dopamine D1 receptors underpin this disengaging property of dopamine signaling, as we demonstrate a D1 agonist shortens both self-stimulation hold-downs and bouts of consummatory behavior. Altogether, we uncover an anatomically defined role of dopamine, which is to disengage its own reinforcing properties through D1 receptor signaling.

abstract: Metabolic enzymes are increasingly recognized for "moonlighting" functions beyond their primary metabolic roles. While such non-canonical activities are well characterized in cancer biology, their roles in innate immunity remain poorly defined. Here, we show that Hexokinase II (HK2), a rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis, suppresses STING-mediated innate immune responses independently of its enzymatic activity. Upon STING activation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) trigger the dissociation of HK2 from the mitochondria to the cytosol. Cytosolic HK2 then interacts with STING, impeding its oligomerization and translocation to the Golgi apparatus, thereby dampening downstream immune signaling. Notably, HK-TAT, a peptide that induces HK2 release from the mitochondria, effectively inhibits STING-dependent immune activation and ameliorates disease phenotypes in STING-driven autoimmune mouse models. Our findings highlight the moonlighting role of HK2 as a negative regulator of STING signaling and provide a potential therapeutic approach for treating autoimmune diseases driven by STING dysregulation.

abstract: Neuronal activity causes topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B) to form DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) within the promoters of early response genes (ERGs), such as Fos and Npas4. TOP2B-mediated DSBs facilitate ERG transcription, yet how this occurs is unclear. Using circular chromosome conformation capture (4C-seq), we report here that DSB formation is sufficient to emulate contact profiles observed at the promoters of Fos and Npas4 following neuronal stimulation, including elevated interactions with their cognate enhancers. Despite their purported risk, recurrent DSB cycles progressively potentiate ERG induction in mouse cortical neurons and HEK293T cells, evoking the effects of transcriptional memory. Potentiated ERG inducibility following recurrent DSBs persists through intervening cell cycles, occurs even when DNA repair is likely mutagenic, and correlates with a substantial loss of cis- and a gain of trans-, chromosomal interactions with ERG promoters. Together, these results reveal how activity-induced DSBs impact transcription by regulating chromatin dynamics at ERG promoters.

abstract: Effective survival after injury requires the precise coordination of immune activation and tissue regeneration, yet the molecular mechanisms balancing these opposing processes remain poorly understood. Here, we identify proline transporters as key regulators of this trade-off in plants. Genetic disruption of two wound-induced proline transporters, ProT2 and ProT3, enhances regenerative capacity and abolishes salicylic acid (SA)-mediated suppression of regeneration while preserving SA-responsive gene expression and SA-mediated antibacterial resistance. Mechanistically, a ProT3-CPK1 complex modulates wound-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS), sustaining a ROS level that restricts de novo root regeneration (DNRR) after wounding. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of proline transport functionally separates immune activation from regenerative suppression and promotes regeneration across multiple plant species. These findings support the role of proline transporters as a regulatory hub integrating stress-induced proline metabolism, SA signaling, and ROS homeostasis to coordinate immunity and regeneration, and highlight chemical inhibition of proline transport as a strategy to improve regeneration without compromising immune defense.

abstract: DNA replication dilutes parental histones and their post-translational modifications, requiring restoration of epigenetic marks on newly incorporated histones. H3K9me3 restoration is unusually slow, extending into the following G1 phase, but the mechanisms governing this delay remain unclear. Here, we show that RIF1 reassociation with heterochromatin during mitotic exit establishes a permissive chromatin environment for histone methyltransferases to resume H3K9me3 deposition. RIF1 promotes recruitment of SUV39H1 and HP1α/β and the increase of H3K9 tri-methylation during G1. RIF1 also recruits protein phosphatase 1α (PP1α) to heterochromatin, and RIF1-PP1α interaction is essential for the maintenance of H3K9me3 levels. Moreover, RIF1-PP1 complex temporally restrains the activity of Aurora kinase at heterochromatin, preventing premature H3S10 phosphorylation before replication and creating a permissive time-window for SUV39H-mediated reinstatement of H3K9me3.

abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. The histone-like nucleoid structuring protein H-NS is an NAP acting as a global regulator of stress genes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. To investigate the regulatory interplay between these two proteins, we examined transcription, DNA binding, and chromatin structure at two regulated operons, hdeAB and proVWX, in E. coli following exposure to acid and salt shock. Our results show that H-NS senses pH and osmotic cues to remodel chromatin and relieve repression, while StpA-in part-compensates for H-NS loss, particularly at proVWX, highlighting a coordinated regulatory network.

abstract: The RNA-binding protein T cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA1) regulates cellular stress responses and tau pathology, key contributors to the pathophysiology of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). TIA1 acts in peripheral monocytes to inhibit inflammation, but its function in central microglia, critical to neuroinflammation and disease progression, remains unknown. Here, we crossed TIA1 microglial conditional knockout (cKO) mice (using a Cx3cr1-driven Cre element) with the PS19 P301S MAPT mouse model of tauopathy and demonstrated that TIA1 promotes microglial activation, with a corresponding suppression of microglia activation upon TIA1cKO. We observe striking reductions in cytokine (Tnf-α and Il-1β) and sensome markers (Clec7a, Trem2, and Itgax); importantly, these reductions were accompanied by decreases in tau pathology. Proteomic analyses show TIA1 interaction with the microglial proteins C1Q, previously implicated in microglial activation. These results position TIA1 as a regulator of neuroinflammation and tauopathy in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells, including microglia, with potentially divergent functions in central versus peripheral immune compartments.

abstract: Ecological communities are reorganizing rapidly under accelerating global change, yet predicting how species assemble, persist, or collapse remains a major challenge.1,2,3,4 Most species distribution models treat species as independent entities, overlooking the dependencies that structure ecological communities. Here, we introduce a language-model-inspired approach5,6 to species distribution that generates ecological communities sequentially, predicting each species and its biomass conditional on previously assembled species. Trained on ∼27,000 reef fish surveys,7 the generative framework reveals multiple coherent community configurations emerging under identical environmental conditions.8,9 For instance, the model can generate both coral-associated and macroalgal-associated fish communities, consistent with alternative ecological regimes described in these ecosystems. The model also uncovers a hierarchy of emergent species positions within the learned dependency structure, including core species strongly associated with particular environmental conditions, bridging species linking alternative configurations, and satellite species occupying more peripheral positions. Despite this richer representation of ecological communities, the model also improves predictions of species occurrence and biomass relative to a species-by-species machine-learning baseline (XGBoost10) and a multispecies deep-learning baseline (MLP11). Together, these results show that ecological communities can be learned and generated as a structured syntax, from which multistability, directional assembly patterns, and hierarchical species positions naturally emerge.

abstract: Convergence and extension (C&E) cell movements promote anteroposterior axis extension and narrow both neuroectodermal and mesodermal tissues during gastrulation. Mediolateral cell intercalation is largely responsible for this morphogenetic process in vertebrates, but evidence suggests that additional cell-extrinsic forces generated by surrounding tissues contribute to the shaping of many structures. In zebrafish, for example, mechanical forces generated by the anteriorly migrating prechordal plate cooperate with tissue-autonomous cell intercalations to promote extension of the notochord. Here, we propose a novel model for notochord morphogenesis by which epiboly forces within the enveloping layer are transmitted to the posterior end of the notochord via a cluster of dorsal forerunner cells (DFCs) that physically links the two. We found that scattering or absence of DFCs caused by loss of crb2a or sox32, respectively, reduces notochord C&E and exacerbates axis extension defects in planar cell polarity signaling-deficient embryos. Using an automated image segmentation and cell shape analysis pipeline, we show that cells within the posterior notochord fail to properly elongate when DFCs are scattered or absent. Finally, we demonstrate that the loss of crb2a and sox32 fails to disrupt C&E of zebrafish embryonic explants in which no epiboly occurs and all extension is driven by cell-intrinsic behaviors. Together, these findings support a model in which DFCs facilitate mechanical coupling of the enveloping layer to the posterior notochord during epiboly to ensure its robust morphogenesis during gastrulation.

abstract: Hunting and meat consumption are widely considered key drivers of human evolution, and hypotheses about their origins draw on comparisons with our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos. These comparisons typically set up a behavioral dichotomy in which chimpanzees are characterized by cooperative hunting of arboreal primates by male-dominated parties, whereas bonobo hunts are thought to involve the opportunistic targeting of terrestrial ungulates, primarily by individual females.1,2,3 Observations from two habituated bonobo communities at LuiKotale covering 10 years challenge this dichotomy. LuiKotale bonobos hunted both terrestrial ungulates (42%) and arboreal primates (43% of vertebrate prey), with red colobus monkeys comprising the majority of primate prey (77%). Males and females hunted arboreal primates at similar rates, and females accounted for most non-primate captures. Female age affected the hunting frequency of primates and ungulates, with the former being biased to younger and the latter to older females. The prominent role of female bonobos in hunting supports predictions that relate hunting activity to intersexual dominance relations rather than risk aversion, with the dominant sex being more active. Comparing data from neighboring communities revealed differences and suggests that social and environmental parameters affect prey choice by each community in different ways. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that chimpanzee-like, male-biased hunting represents the ancestral condition. They highlight the contribution of females to obtaining vertebrate prey, call for a reassessment of the role of females in hunting and meat sharing, and by extension, the framing of models of early hominin subsistence and social organization.

abstract: Cell-cell communication is indispensable for cell specification and differentiation throughout plant reproduction. The egg cell and its sister synergid cell have long been considered closely coordinated partners during fertilization, yet the nature of this interplay and their specific roles remain unclear. Here, we show that synergid cells could acquire the competence to initiate cell division for embryogenesis following egg cell collapse. Unlike the traditional view, synergid cells appear to take over the egg cell role without undergoing fate conversion to adopt the egg cell identity. These findings suggest that synergid cells possess an intrinsic embryogenic potential, which is specifically unlocked upon egg cell collapse, thus enabling embryogenic initiation in the absence of a functional egg cell. Building on this discovery, we established an in planta haploid-induction system independent of conventional haploid-inducing genes. Importantly, this system also functions in tomato, a distantly related dicotyledonous crop, thus offering a broad conceptual framework for engineering haploid production across diverse plant species.

abstract: The insect central complex governs intricate navigational behaviors. One key region of the central complex, the fan-shaped body (FB), is where movement decisions are computed during goal-directed behaviors. However, our knowledge of when FB circuits are deployed is limited, and the FB has only been directly implicated in a few, narrowly defined behaviors. Here, we demonstrate that FB circuits affect course-correcting movements that, over long timescales, align the fly's heading with the perceived direction of optic flow. Silencing a major input neuronal population to the FB, the PFNd neurons, abolishes this behavior while leaving certain reflexive turning behaviors intact. Further, introduction of a fictive error signal in either the PFNd or PFNa neurons via optogenetic activation reveals that they are sufficient to affect the forward movement of the fly while slightly biasing its heading direction. We propose a model whereby the fly recruits the circuitry of the central complex to selectively influence features of movement that emerge over long timescales.

abstract: Sensory systems comprise ascending pathways that convey information from the sense organs and descending pathways that provide feedback and contextual signals to guide sensory processing. How top-down signals are integrated at early stages to improve sensory function remains poorly understood. The dorsal cochlear nucleus (DCN) is a cerebellum-like circuit proposed to perform adaptive filtering, including suppression of self-generated sounds. A major question is how sound-frequency-specific top-down information is processed by the DCN, since many top-down inputs target granule cells whose axons span the tonotopic axis and are unlikely to maintain frequency-specific signals. Here, we characterize neurons in the inferior colliculus that provide descending input to DCN. We show that among their targets are unipolar brush cells (UBCs) that distribute and transform descending signals directly to principal neurons and inhibitory interneurons in a circuit that bypasses granule cells. In vivo activation of UBCs attenuated auditory responses in awake mice. Together, these findings identify a circuit through which top-down signals from IC could influence early auditory processing and potentially guide adaptive filtering in the DCN.

abstract: For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage’s polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4–6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

abstract: Aminopyrazoles have emerged as a promising series of antileishmanial compounds. Molecular target deconvolution has been a major challenge because successive drug exposure failed to select for resistance. Chemical mutagenesis combined with aminopyrazole selective pressure and whole genome sequencing was used as an alternative approach. From the obtained panel of 28 resistant lines, an association was discovered between >10-49-fold resistance and multiple independent heterozygous mutations in the C-terminal FYVE Zn finger domain of LINF_180011100. LINF_180011100 gene overexpression and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing has independently confirmed the association with 10- to 30-fold aminopyrazole resistance. Genetic fusion with an N-terminal green fluorescent protein tag and partial colocalization with a C-terminal mCherry-tagged small GTPase Rab5 demonstrated that the functional protein primarily localizes in endocytic vesicles. In situ target engagement assays confirmed a selective effect of aminopyrazoles and its abrogation by introducing a resistance-conferring mutation. Finally, a direct interaction between the lead compound and recombinantly produced LINF_180011100 FYVE Zn finger domain was demonstrated through a biophysical assay. Hence, this work formally validates LINF_180011100 as a drug target and resistance determinant for several aminopyrazole leads and provides insights into the mechanism of action.

abstract: Historically, suppressor analysis has been a powerful tool for uncovering the functions of essential genes. In this study, we report Sup-seq, a transposon-sequencing technique with random DNA barcodes that enables genome-wide detection of genetic suppression. When applied to seven essential genes in Streptococcus pneumoniae , Sup-seq revealed 53 suppressors across various cellular pathways. These suppressors function through diverse mechanisms, such as gene inactivation, overexpression, or downregulation, depending on the locations and orientations of the transposon insertions. Our proof-of-concept experiments identified a previously uncharacterized transcriptional regulator that controls chaperone and ribosomal protein expression, as well as a mechanism that bypasses the requirement for acetate kinase for growth. Furthermore, we found that phosphatidylglycerol is conditionally essential in pneumococcus, revealing an unexpected link between phospholipid synthesis and potassium transport. These findings demonstrate that Sup-seq is a facile approach for providing mechanistic insights into the functions of essential genes. Additionally, Sup-seq can be adapted to other bacteria, aiding in the identification of new antimicrobial targets.

abstract: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) governs selective nucleocytoplasmic exchange, yet the spatial organization of its intrinsically disordered FG nucleoporins (FG-Nups) in living cells has remained unresolved. Here we reconstruct the three-dimensional distributions of all eleven mammalian FG-Nups within individual NPCs in live cells by combining high-speed 2D single-molecule tracking with post-localization 2D-to-3D transformation, validated by Monte Carlo simulations and independent 3D MINFLUX measurements. The resulting map reveals that the FG barrier is not a uniform disordered meshwork but a stratified architecture. Five centrally anchored FG-Nups form an annular structure surrounding a sparsely occupied axial corridor, whereas six asymmetrically positioned FG-Nups extend flexibly beyond the scaffold to generate dynamic caps at the cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic faces. Nup214 and Nup153 switch between open and closed axial conformations, whereas Nup98 spans nearly the full pore length and overlaps with most other FG-Nups, linking the major FG zones across the barrier. Together, these features define an adaptable capped channel extending up to ~270 nm across the nuclear envelope, with a ~ 40 nm annular central region and FG extensions reaching ~80–130 nm into the cytoplasm and ~60–100 nm into the nucleoplasm. Transport-route measurements in the same live-cell system show that passive diffusion preferentially traverses the relatively FG-poor central corridor, whereas facilitated transport follows peripheral FG-rich pathways. These findings provide a unified structural framework for NPC selectivity and support a model in which distributed, position-dependent FG architectures, rather than a single central barrier, organize transport.

abstract: Bacterial cell division requires synchronized synthesis of septal peptidoglycan by the glycosyltransferase FtsW and the transpeptidase FtsI within the divisome. How glycan polymerization and peptide crosslinking are coordinated within this assembly remains poorly understood. Here, we provide molecular insights into this coupling in the core divisome complex FtsWIQLB from Vibrio cholerae . By integrating a quantitative, native substrates-based dual-activity assay, cryo-EM, AlphaFold modeling, disulfide trapping, mass spectrometry, and chemical biology, we identify an inactive down and a putative active up conformation of FtsI with distinct interaction networks. We discover a coupling helix in FtsI that directly modulates FtsW processivity. Importantly, crosslinking requires a minimum glycan strand length, consistent with our model of coupling. Lastly, the lipid tail of lipid II is important for FtsW processivity, with short-tail analogs acting as inhibitors. Our findings suggest that substrate-driven conformational switching of FtsI spatially and temporally couples these essential enzymatic activities.

abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired by Ku-dependent non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or DNA end resection-dependent homologous recombination (HR). Previously, it was shown that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 can remove Ku from DSBs and initiate resection, showing flexibility in DSB repair pathway choice. However, which NHEJ intermediates can be disrupted by resection factors remains unknown. Using reconstituted reactions with purified S. cerevisiae proteins, we show here that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 is not directly inhibited by any of the core NHEJ factors. Instead, we find that MRX-pSae2 is inhibited structurally. DNA synapsis, a dynamic NHEJ intermediate that bridges DSBs, strongly suppresses resection. Non-ligatable ends are refractory to MRX-pSae2 once synapsis formed, and NHEJ assemblies with catalytic mutants of DNA ligase IV that permit synapsis but do not allow ligation likewise inhibit resection. We further demonstrate that removal of Ku from DSBs requires RPA, which interacts with MRX and pSae2 to synergistically stimulate MRX 3′−5′ exonuclease activity, generating free 3′ overhangs. Our data support a model in which DNA synapsis temporarily prevents resection, allowing NHEJ to execute ligation. If ligation fails and synapsis dissociates, MRX-pSae2 and RPA promote resection that removes non-productive NHEJ assemblies and channels DSB repair toward HR. The data help explain the suppression of NHEJ by RPA observed in previous genetic experiments.

abstract: Carbapenems are last line β lactam antibiotics for multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections, yet the adaptive routes by which Enterobacterales survive carbapenem stress remain incompletely understood. Here we show that prolonged subinhibitory meropenem exposure promotes O antigen loss in Klebsiella pneumoniae , predominantly via insertion sequence-mediated disruption of O-antigen biosynthesis genes, thereby enhancing carbapenem resistance. O-antigen deficiency is accompanied by envelope-associated redox remodeling and reprogramming of central metabolism, mitigating meropenem-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation and oxidative killing. This adaptation also conferred collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides, associated with increased outer-membrane electronegativity and altered porin expression that may promote aminoglycoside uptake. Analysis of public genomes further revealed O-antigen locus disruptions in subsets of K. pneumoniae and Escherichia coli isolates. Together, our findings establish O-antigen deficiency as a surface-remodeling adaptation that enhances carbapenem resistance through coordinated metabolic and redox reprogramming, while exposing an aminoglycoside vulnerability that warrants further evaluation.

abstract: Understanding rising atmospheric CO 2 effects on the chemistry of the world’s ecosystems remains nascent. CO 2 dissolved in water forms carbonic acid, thereby lowering pH (ocean acidification [OA]). Diatoms, which generate 40% of ocean primary productivity, depend on dissolved silicon to construct their silica frustules; lower pH reduces silica (SiO 2 ) solubility in seawater. Recent experiments document enhanced silica sedimentation under elevated CO 2 , implying reduced Si recycling and availability to support diatom production at the ecosystem scale. We tested this hypothesis using long-term data from a productive Pacific coastline undergoing rapid pH decline. Over two decades, as pH declined, dissolved Si:N and water column chlorophyll concurrently declined strongly. Accounting for variation in potential Si transport vectors did not change these relationships. Our results support the OA Si loss hypothesis and indicate that this process is already ongoing in some productive ocean regions, with implications for the carbon cycle, coastal food webs, and human well-being.

abstract: Blood phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) accurately detects Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology but is also elevated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), likely reflecting peripheral (big) tau released from muscle. Assays selectively measuring brain-derived (BD-) tau and BD-p-tau217 are therefore needed. We analysed serum BD-tau and p-tau217 in ALS ( n = 139), AD ( n = 101) and controls ( n = 75) using direct immunoassays and after BD-Tau immunoprecipitation (BD-Tau-IP), and tau species in brain ( n = 16), spinal cord ( n = 11) and muscle ( n = 10) by targeted mass spectrometry. With the direct immunoassays, BD-tau and p-tau217 were increased in AD and ALS versus controls. After BD-Tau-IP, BD-tau and BD-p-tau217 were elevated in AD only, improving diagnostic accuracy. Mass spectrometry revealed a central-to-peripheral shift from BD-tau to big tau predominance, with exclusively big p-tau217 detected in muscle. Selective detection of BD-tau species improves the specificity of blood AD biomarkers by reducing peripheral tau confounding.

abstract: Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) is a global pathogen, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing its virulence and antimicrobial resistance are poorly understood. Here, we characterize 370 transcription factors (TFs) and their binding profiles in a clinical isolate CR-HvKP4, and construct a global gene regulatory network. Using topological analysis, we identify and validate key virulence and antibiotic resistance regulators. Temporal transcriptomic profiling reveals a highly streamlined regulatory efficiency, where over 88% of TFs maintain steady-state expression across growth phases, with middle-layer TFs exhibiting preferential high-level expression to process regulatory signals. Additionally, our pan-genome study across 2059 KP strains reveals high conservation of TFs and distinct geographic patterns within sequence types. Finally, we develop a predictive model that accurately maps transcriptional regulation across independent KP strains. Collectively, we identify 25 key TFs and four TFs regulons at two growth stages, highlighting VmrR (RS15210), whose deletion significantly attenuated virulence in the lungs of female mice.

abstract: Gallstone disease is a highly prevalent and costly gastrointestinal disease. Yet, genetic variation in gallstone susceptibility and its implication in metabolic pathways remain to be explored. We report a trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease including 100,856 cases and 1,596,602 controls in the UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan, and Million Veteran Program. We identified 116 (59 novel) risk loci across meta-analysis and found replication in statistically compelling signals in the All of Us Research Program. A polygenic risk score constructed from trans-ancestry lead variants was positively associated with liver chemistry and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and negatively associated with total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein levels among trans-ancestry and European ancestry groups in the Penn Medicine BioBank. Colocalization of risk loci with 44 traits and with expression quantitative trait loci from eight tissues yielded 321 and 110 significant colocalizations, respectively. These findings broaden our understanding of the genetic architecture of gallstone disease.

abstract: X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is essential for extraembryonic tissue growth and embryo development in mice. However, species-specific differences in its timing and regulation have left its role in human development unclear. Here, we show that the in vitro differentiation of naive human pluripotent stem cells to trophoblast stem cells and extraembryonic mesoderm cells is accompanied by XCI. The inactive X chromosome displays an atypical chromatin state, lacking DNA methylation and canonical heterochromatin marks. We demonstrate that extraembryonic differentiation and XCI are temporally linked. Using loss of function approaches, we found that XIST is required for XCI establishment in humans. Furthermore, we show that XCI is needed for the survival of human female extraembryonic cells. Together, these findings link XCI to the formation of human extraembryonic lineages, with important implications for human reproductive biology.

abstract: Biological systems exhibit complex hierarchical regulation, with interactions across multiple layers governing transitions between states. Identifying the causal architecture underlying these state transitions remains challenging because confounding can produce spurious associations in observational data. Here we present CauTrigger, a hierarchical deep latent variable model that integrates do-calculus to identify potential causal triggers and predict perturbation outcomes across multiple regulatory layers. By disentangling causal and spurious latent factors, CauTrigger recursively reconstructs the underlying regulatory hierarchy and enables interpretable reasoning from observational data. Across synthetic and real-world datasets with multilayer regulatory structures, CauTrigger outperforms existing methods in identifying causal triggers and forecasting system-level responses. Applied to single-cell multi-omics and gut microbiome datasets, CauTrigger prioritizes candidate causal triggers and uses in silico perturbations to generate testable hypotheses about biological state transitions and inform potential strategies for state navigation. Together, these results establish CauTrigger as a general-purpose framework for causal discovery in complex biological systems.

abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR–Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo 2 , Trpv 1 and Scn9a ) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Na v ) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.

abstract: Flexible cognition requires the brain to generalize across tasks while preserving task-specific information. Previous work showed that task representations are compressed in the association cortex and expanded in sensory and motor systems, but the mechanisms underlying these transformations are unclear. Here we test whether the geometry of intrinsic brain connectivity constrains how representations change between cortical regions. We analyzed functional MRI acquired during 16 diverse cognitive tasks together with activity flow modeling, finding that connectivity dimensionality predicts representational changes across the cortex. Low-dimensional connectivity compressed task representations and increased similarities across tasks, whereas high-dimensional connectivity expanded representations and supported conjunctive coding of task features. Activity flow modeling reproduced the observed compression-to-expansion pattern along the sensory–association–motor hierarchy and generated representational geometries that more closely matched targets than sources, consistent with transformation rather than transfer of information. These findings identify network geometry as a systems-level principle that shapes cortical representations and supports flexible cognition.

abstract: Feeding begins with food-seeking and ends with nutrient absorption and waste elimination. Although meal-related sensory cues shape feeding behavior, how they engage neural circuits to control digestion remains unclear. We dissected vagal gut-brain-gut pathways mediating meal-induced gastric secretion. Stomach-innervating vagal afferents were necessary and sufficient for secretion. Among them, Glp1r+ and Sst+ neurons drove acid, pepsin, and gastrin secretion, whereas Oxtr+ and Vip+ neurons had little effect. Piezo2 was expressed in Glp1r+ mechanosensory afferents, and conditional deletion of Piezo2 attenuated distension-evoked secretion. On the efferent limb, genetically defined vagal motor-neuron subsets showed distinct secretory effects: Cck+ neurons broadly increased acid, pepsin, and gastrin, whereas Grp+ neurons preferentially affected acid secretion. Finally, enteric circuit dissection revealed modular output control, with Calb2+ neurons driving secretion with minimal motility effects. Together, these results define a cell-type-resolved vagal-enteric architecture for gastric control.

abstract: Periodontal disease involves persistent inflammation and alveolar bone loss. Photobiomodulation using light-emitting diodes (LEDs) may regulate inflammation and bone remodelling, but the optimal wavelength and irradiation timing remain unclear. Human gingival fibroblasts and RAW 264.7 macrophages were irradiated with 525, 630, or 850 nm LED light before or after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation. The effects of 630 nm irradiation were further evaluated in primary mouse calvarial osteoblasts, MC3T3-E1 cells, bone marrow-derived macrophages, and RAW 264.7 osteoclast precursors. Inflammatory mediators, nitric oxide production, cell viability, osteoblast differentiation, and osteoclast formation were assessed. Among the wavelengths tested, 630 nm irradiation most consistently reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and secretion and decreased nitric oxide production without affecting cell viability. In primary osteoblasts and MC3T3-E1 cells, 630 nm irradiation at 5 and 10 J/cm² increased alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, osteogenic marker expression, RUNX2 protein levels, and Smad1/5/9 phosphorylation. In contrast, the same irradiation conditions did not significantly affect osteoclast differentiation or the expression of osteoclast-related markers. Irradiation with 630 nm LED light suppressed inflammatory responses and promoted osteoblast differentiation without enhancing osteoclastogenesis. These findings suggest that 630 nm photobiomodulation may provide a balanced therapeutic approach for periodontal disease, although further validation in animal models and clinical studies is required.

abstract: How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

abstract: The accurate localization of charging holes is an indispensable perception step for the automatic charging system of electric vehicles, since the success of subsequent charging-gun insertion depends directly on the precise estimation of the geometric centers of the holes on the vehicle charging interface. This paper presents a lightweight machine-vision framework for charging hole localization based on contour-driven detection and geometric verification. The proposed framework integrates image filtering, RGB-to-HSL color-space conversion, parameterized HSL adjustment, two-stage contour detection, minimum enclosing circle fitting, and Hough circle verification into a deterministic pipeline. The framework is interpretable, does not require a learning-based training process, and can be deployed on conventional CPU-based computing resources. The image data used in this study were acquired by a monocular RGB camera mounted on the charging robot end-effector, in the same sensing configuration in which the system is intended to operate. A total of 80 images were collected from six vehicles equipped with the same five-hole charging interface, under realistic variations of illumination, viewing angle, reflective interference, and background complexity. Detailed parameter selection rationale, a parameter perturbation analysis, and a condition-specific ablation analysis are reported. On an Intel Core i7-12700 CPU with 16 GB RAM and no GPU acceleration, the proposed framework achieves an overall mean localization error of 4.2 pixels and a 96.25% detection success rate, with an average per-image processing time of approximately 60 ms. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides accurate, robust, and engineering-deployable charging-hole localization for the target charging interface.

title: An environmental type-recessiveness framework for the spatial coupling of environmental heterogeneity and ICH recessiveness in Guizhou's ethnic minority villages, China.

abstract: The relationship between environmental heterogeneity and intangible cultural heritage (ICH) remains insufficiently explored at the regional scale. Using data from 312 ethnic minority villages and 305 ICH items in Guizhou, China, this study develops an Environmental Type-Recessiveness Cultural Adaptation (ERC) framework to examine associations between environmental conditions and ICH distribution patterns. Four environmental variables were integrated into five environmental types using K-means clustering. ICH recessiveness was operationalized as a three-dimensional composite index comprising observability, carrier explicitness, and environmental association. Expert scoring exhibited strong reliability. Results reveal clear associations between environmental settings and ICH recessiveness: moderate recessiveness predominates across the province; high-elevation, high-elevation environments with large distance to water systems tend to host more recessive forms of heritage, whereas low-relief and highly accessible landscapes are associated with lower recessiveness. These findings indicate that environmental differentiation is spatially coupled with systematic variation in ICH recessiveness. Such spatial correspondence is consistent with processes of socio-ecological adaptation rather than environmental determinism. The ERC framework provides a standardized and reproducible quantitative approach for comparative analysis of ICH across heterogeneous landscapes, offering a transferable tool for heritage research in mountainous and ethnically diverse regions. Overall, the observed west-to-east gradient in ICH recessiveness further supports the role of socio-ecological adaptation in shaping ethnic heritage patterns in mountainous environments.

title: Assessing the impact of phylogenetic reconstruction error on genetic reassortment inference in segmented viruses.

author_details.name: Castelán-Sánchez HG
author_details.affiliation: Department of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine, Western University, London, Ontario, Canada.

author_details.name: Poon AFY

abstract: Recombination is an important process in the evolution of RNA viruses. For viruses with segmented genomes, recombination can occur by reassortment of entire genomic segments. This process has played a significant role in the adaptation and spread of influenza viruses with novel genomic combinations, i.e., antigenic shifts. Reassortment is usually identified by discrepancies between the topologies of trees reconstructed from different genomic segments, e.g., subtree prune and regraft (SPR) rearrangements. However, this phylogenetic discordance can also result from errors in tree reconstruction due to insufficient information. The objective of this study was to evaluate the contribution of phylogenetic reconstruction error to the inference of reassortment events from influenza A virus (IAV) genomes from avian hosts. We curated a dataset of 11,795 complete avian H5Nx IAV genomes and sampled subsets of HA sequences with different expected levels of reconstruction error. Next, we simulated molecular evolution along the trees reconstructed from these HA samples, varying rates of evolution and sequence lengths to correspond to the other genomic segments. Because these simulations had no reassortment, any phylogenetic discordance identified from the resulting trees must be caused by reconstruction error. We found that simulations from random samples yielded about 32% as many SPRs as obtained from real data. This false positive rate was reduced to 4% when simulating trees from the most genetically divergent subset of HA sequences. By modifying the simulated trees with SPR rearrangements, we observed a false negative rate of 8.5%, which increased with the number of SPRs per tree. Overall, we found that reassortment can be substantially overestimated from phylogenetic discordance, underscoring the need to account for phylogenetic uncertainty and sampling design when analyzing IAV datasets for reassortment.

abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a fluctuating confusional state occurring early after surgery. Given its fluctuating nature, POD detection is influenced by the frequency and timing of screening. Sparse assessments potentially underestimate the true incidence reported in individual studies, subsequently influencing the weight of studies in meta-analyses, and the results and precision of these meta-analyses. To develop a method to evaluate the robustness of meta-analyses to the variation in the frequency and timing of POD assessment across included studies. We developed an expert-based scoring system to rate studies according to the confidence that a patient reported not to have POD in the study truly did not, based on the reported timing and frequency of POD assessments. We describe how to use the system to generate hypothetical event rates for studies if the frequency and timing of POD assessment were optimal and how to use these rates in a sensitivity analysis of meta-analyses including these studies. We illustrate the method applying it to two meta-analyses as work examples, one of observational studies and one of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). In our work examples, the expert-based score for the individual studies ranged from 33-77% for the observational and 22-70% for RCTs meta-analysis. Sensitivity analyses showed a change in the pooled effect size, heterogeneity, and precision compared to the original estimates. We present a method to evaluate the robustness of a meta-analysis of studies having POD as an outcome, when there is variation across individual studies in the frequency and timing of POD assessment. The confidence score acts as a preliminary index of the robustness of meta-analyses. Through work examples, we showed that the robustness depends on the characteristics of individual studies included.

title: Association among Dietary Inflammatory Index, sleep quality and nutritional status in fixed daytime and rotating shift workers.

author_details.name: Sünbül Ş
author_details.affiliation: Department of Nutrition and Dietetics, Faculty of Health Sciences, Ankara University, Ankara, Türkiye.; Kalecik Vocational School, Food Technology Program, Ankara University, Ankara, Türkiye.

abstract: Shift work is associated with irregular eating behaviors, increased energy intake, and impaired sleep quality. Poor dietary patterns may elevate systemic inflammation, contributing to long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risks. The aim of this study was to investigate differences in the Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII), sleep quality, dietary intake, and anthropometric and body composition measures between fixed daytime workers and rotating shift workers and to examine the associations among these parameters. This cross-sectional study included 52 male workers employed at a defense industry factory in Ankara, Türkiye, who worked either fixed daytime or rotating shifts. Dietary intake was assessed using 24-h dietary recalls for three non-consecutive days, from which macronutrient and micronutrient intakes were calculated. DII scores were computed to assess the inflammatory potential of the diet. Sleep quality was evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Anthropometric measurements, body composition, blood pressure, and biochemical parameters, including fasting plasma glucose, lipid profile (total cholesterol, HDL-C, LDL-C, and triglycerides), C-reactive protein, and homocysteine, were measured using standardised protocols. Rotating shift workers had significantly higher total energy intake and higher daily intakes of fructose, total fat, saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids, cholesterol, and several micronutrients, including vitamin A, folate, iron, calcium, and phosphorus compared with fixed daytime workers (p < 0.05). Mean DII scores did not differ significantly between the groups (Fixed daytime: 0.2 ± 1.86; rotating shift: -0.2 ± 2.25). DII scores were positively correlated with global PSQI score (r = 0.278, p = 0.046), the PSQI sleep duration component score (r = 0.319, p = 0.021), and daytime dysfunction component score (r = 0.287, p = 0.039); however, the association between DII and overall sleep quality was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounding factors (age, BMI, smoking status, physical activity, and work schedule). These findings suggest that dietary habits, pro-inflammatory dietary patterns, and poor sleep quality may represent co-existing factors associated with metabolic risk, and addressing these factors may contribute to better overall metabolic health.

abstract: Diabetic Neuropathy (DN) is a prevalent complication of diabetes linked to chronic inflammation. Interleukin-6 (IL-6) and Interleukin-10 (IL-10) are key cytokines implicated in DN pathogenesis. This study investigates the association of IL6 and IL10 gene polymorphisms and serum levels with DN in the Bangladeshi population. A case-control study was conducted with 225 participants: diabetic patients with DN (n = 75), diabetic patients without DN (n = 75), and healthy controls (n = 75). Genomic DNA was extracted for genotyping IL-6 (rs1800796) and IL-10 (rs1800896) SNPs via PCR. Serum cytokine levels were measured using ELISA. Serum IL-6 levels were significantly higher in the DN group than in the other study groups (p < 0.0001), with the highest levels observed among individuals with the IL-6 rs1800796 CC genotype. In unadjusted analyses, the IL-6 CC genotype was associated with increased odds of DN compared with healthy controls (OR = 4.813, 95% CI: 1.752-13.85, p = 0.0040), as was the IL-10 GG genotype (OR = 2.679, 95% CI: 1.000-6.751, p = 0.0373). However, neither IL-6 nor IL-10 genotype remained independently associated with DN after multivariable adjustment. Serum IL-10 levels did not differ significantly among the study groups (p = 0.0948). Combined genotype analyses showed several nominal associations, although these findings were exploratory. Serum IL-6 showed promising discriminatory ability in distinguishing patients with DN from the other study groups, whereas IL-10 demonstrated limited discriminatory performance. These findings support further investigation of serum IL-6 as a potential candidate biomarker for diabetic neuropathy, whereas the independent contribution of the investigated IL-6 and IL-10 polymorphisms remains uncertain. Larger prospective studies with independent external validation are required before clinical application can be considered.

title: Can immersive virtual reality be an alternative world for eliciting consumer willingness to pay for food?

author_details.name: Nakajima T

abstract: This study examines whether consumers' willingness to pay (WTP) for ready-to-eat cereals differs between immersive virtual reality (IVR) and real-world (RW) environments. Real choice experiments were conducted with 227 respondents who selected reservation dates without knowing whether they corresponded to the IVR or RW setting. To derive consumers' WTP, random parameter logit models were estimated primarily in WTP space, while preference-space models were used as a robustness check. The results show no significant differences in WTP between IVR and RW for any of the cereal products tested. This suggests that consumers' product choices in IVR environments are based on monetary valuations, similar to those in real environments. When combined with real economic incentives, IVR-based choice experiments may therefore yield WTP estimates comparable to those obtained from conventional real choice experiments. To our knowledge, this is the first study to compare WTP between IVR and RW environments using an incentive-compatible experimental design.

abstract: Hypoxanthine guanine xanthine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGXPRT) is one of the central enzymes of purine salvage pathway of protozoan parasites, including Plasmodium. These parasites are purine auxotrophs, and rely on purine salvage pathway for nucleic acid synthesis. Inhibiting the enzymatic activity can effectively reduce the parasite- induced infections, including malaria. In this context, a library of new carbothioamide derivatives 1-17 of paroxetine was synthesized via single-step chemical transformation strategy with a series of substituted phenyl isothiocyanates. All compounds were purified, and their structures were deduced by using spectroscopic techniques, such as mass, FT-IR, UV, and 1H-, and 13C-NMR. These compounds were evaluated for their HGXPRT inhibitory activity via in vitro UV-based spectrophotometric assay. All derivatives 1-17 showed varying potential to inhibit the enzyme activity with IC50 values between 19.0 to 76.9 µM, with highest activity showed by compound 13 (IC50 = 19.0 ± 2.09 µM) within the series, but remained less potent than the standard (9-deazaguanine, IC50 = 12.00 ± 1.0 µM). Biophysical, molecular docking, and molecular simulation studies were carried out further to analyse the enzyme-inhibitor interaction, and stability. These compounds were predicted to occupy the putative allosteric site of enzyme. Furthermore, cytotoxic profile of these compounds were also evaluated via ADMET analysis and MTT assay, and found to be largely non-cytotoxic. The current study has identified potential hits against HGXPRT enzyme that could further be investigated as anti-parasitic drugs.

title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation.

author_details.name: Dahle S
author_details.affiliation: Department of Physics, Norwegian University of Life Sciences, Ås, Norway.

author_details.name: Ness TV

abstract: There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

title: CohAlign: Predicting the first-order noise susceptibility of gradients in equivariant quantum neural networks.

author_details.name: Ugail H
author_details.affiliation: Centre for Visual Computing and Intelligent Systems, University of Bradford, Bradford, United Kingdom.

author_details.name: Howard N
author_details.affiliation: School of Individualized Study, Rochester Institute of Technology, Rochester, New York, United States of America.

abstract: Quantum neural networks learn by following gradients, and on real hardware those gradients are washed out by noise. Predicting how quickly this happens, before any finite noise experiment or circuit sweep is run, remains an open problem. We present CohAlign, an open source toolkit that computes the first order noise susceptibility of the ensemble second moment of a specified parameter gradient in a charge conserving brickwork quantum neural network. The computation needs only a classical description of the circuit, the noise model, the prepared state, the readout and the initialisation prior. The predicted quantity is distinct from training convergence or final accuracy. The key observation is that only the part of the noise that a measurement can actually see matters. A purposefully constructed control channel makes this clear, damaging the operator carrying a gradient at nearly the maximal rate while the measured gradient remains exactly as predicted and untouched. We validate the predictions against separately evaluated finite difference slopes across the benchmark suite, including a signed coherent case, in exact simulations at eight and ten qubits and on two circuit topologies.

abstract: Postoperative pain after cesarean section may delay recovery and impair function. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) and low-level laser photobiomodulation (PBM) are used for pain control, but the additional effect of combining these therapies remains unclear. This study investigated this effect. A randomized clinical trial with four groups: combined TENS + low-level laser photobiomodulation (PBM), TENS alone, placebo, and control. Assessments were performed at 8-12 h (t1), 20-24 h (t2), and 44-48 h postpartum (t3). Outcomes included pain intensity, functional independence, functional capacity assessed by the Two-Minute Walk Test (2MWT), and cardiorespiratory variables. Two intervention sessions were applied after t1 and t2, except in the control group. Data were analyzed using mixed ANOVA and nonparametric equivalents when appropriate. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. A total of 88 women were included. Pain intensity decreased significantly over time in the combined TENS + PBM group (1.82 ± 1.18 at t2 vs 1.30 ± 0.86 at t3; p = 0.008) and in the TENS group (1.59 ± 1.05 at t2 vs 0.95 ± 1.05 at t3; p = 0.025). Functional independence increased in the combined therapy group (14.9 ± 3.3 at t1 vs 17.1 ± 3.6 at t3; p = 0.034) and in the TENS group (15.2 ± 3.0 at t1 vs 17.5 ± 3.4 at t3; p = 0.028). Functional capacity improved in all groups between t2 and t3 in the Two-Minute Walk Test (Control: 63.5 vs 76.8 m, p = 0.002; Placebo: 50.3 vs 63.9 m, p = 0.002; Combined: 48.3 vs 65.2 m, p = 0.0006; TENS: 61.1 vs 72.2 m, p = 0.005). No significant differences were observed between groups (p > 0.05). A significant time effect was found for pain (p < 0.05) and functional independence (p < 0.001). Pain decreased and functional independence improved during the postoperative period. However, the combination of TENS and low-level laser photobiomodulation did not provide additional benefits compared with the other groups.

abstract: Deep-learning-based holographic reconstruction requires numerical data with reliable ground truth for training and quantitative evaluation. Experimental hologram acquisition and pixel-level phase annotation can be difficult to control, making physically defined numerical cases useful as reproducible benchmarks. Here, three analytically specified phase targets-a smooth Gaussian distribution, a four-level step distribution, and a radially structured Siemens Star-are used to generate off-axis digital holograms with known phase ground truth. A frequency-domain filtering procedure is applied before inverse Fourier reconstruction, followed by DCT-based global phase unwrapping. Reconstruction quality is quantified using root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), correlation coefficient, and profile-based error analysis. The results show that reconstruction errors are comparatively small in smooth regions and increase near abrupt or high-spatial-frequency phase transitions. The three cases are therefore presented as controlled benchmark examples for algorithm verification and baseline comparison, not as a complete substitute for experimental holographic datasets or as a complete training corpus for deep-learning models.

abstract: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome, driven by trauma or infection, involves excessive innate immune activation. Dexamethasone (DEX), a synthetic glucocorticoid, suppresses inflammation, although adverse side effects limit its clinical use. The inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that assembles in response to inflammatory stimuli like ATP after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) priming, facilitates caspase-1 cleavage and release of the proinflammatory cytokine, interleukin (IL)-1β. We investigated whether DEX and decanoic acid (DA), a saturated medium-chain fatty acid, inhibited caspase-1 activity and IL-1β release in an LPS/ATP-stimulated THP-1 macrophage model and whether co-treatment would allow for pharmacologic DEX dose-sparing in vitro. PMA-differentiated THP-1macrophages were primed with LPS overnight and stimulated with ATP for 3 h in the presence of DA, DEX, or both. Viability and cytotoxicity were assessed. Caspase-1 activity and IL-1β were quantified, and EC50 values were calculated by nonlinear regression. In control conditions, LPS/ATP stimulation induced 5.56 (q1: 3.51 - q3: 6.38) ng/mL of IL-1β release. DA and DEX inhibited IL-1β with full dose-response EC50 values of 131.7 μM and 24.29 nM, respectively. DA concentrations exceeding 800 μM decreased cell viability. An 8 x 9-point DA/DEX dose matrix (0-500 μM DA; 0 to 1e4 nM DEX) was used to interrogate drug interaction for IL-1β inhibition and caspase-1 activity. DEX EC50 values remained within a narrow 95% confidence interval of 17.5-26.6 nM, regardless of DA background concentration. DA reduced caspase-1 enzymatic activity with a calculated EC50 value of ~140 μM; whereas, DEX did not. These data show that DA and DEX act independently. Furthermore, compared to DEX alone, the presence of DA allowed for equivalent in vitro IL-1β suppression at lower DEX concentrations, supporting pharmacologic DEX dose-sparing. Determination of whether this pharmacologic effect translates to clinically meaningful corticosteroid dose reduction requires further study.

abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) has emerged as an impactful tool for controlling advanced prosthetic devices by detecting and recording muscle electrical activity during motion. This study presents a unique technique for recognizing nine distinct classes of finger movements by utilizing the Ninapro database. To address an underexplored domain of upper-limb prosthetic control, this research targets fine-resolution individual finger movements rather than the broad range of hand gestures. A custom-made one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) was developed and validated using a within-subject evaluation strategy and signals. The proposed model achieved an overall classification accuracy of 90.1%. An in-depth sensitivity/specificity analysis for each finger movement class was administered to gain key insights into current recognition capabilities. The findings presented in this study demonstrate the viability of fine-resolution finger-movement recognition, offering foundational insights that may inform the future development and refinement of control systems in the prosthetic field.

abstract: Competency-based education (CBE) is gaining prominence in post-secondary education due to its effectiveness in optimizing workforce readiness. However, assessing competence and workforce readiness presents a significant challenge. Entrustable professional activities (EPAs) offer a promising solution by translating competencies into observable, entrustable tasks. While EPAs have been widely adopted in clinical training, their application in non-clinical educational contexts remains minimal. Guided by Rogers' Diffusion of Innovation theory, this scoping review aims to map the diffusion of EPAs beyond medical education and examine their scalability to non-clinical educational contexts, where real-world practice errors may undermine system integrity, educational outcomes, or public trust. This review will progress through five stages following Arksey and O'Malley's framework. Searches will be conducted across Ovid MEDLINE, CINAHL, Scopus, ERIC, and Google Scholar. The research question is: "How have EPAs been adapted, developed and implemented outside of medical education, and what factors influence their adoption in non-clinical educational contexts?" The search will include studies that describe, evaluate, or reflect on the adaptation, development, or implementation of EPAs outside medical education, and exclude studies that only propose, define, or discuss EPAs, focus on medical education, or are not published in English. Titles and abstracts will be reviewed first, followed by the full-text examination of relevant studies. Data will be extracted and summarized to highlight key findings. A two-reviewer protocol will ensure quality during screening and data extraction. The findings from this review may provide practical guidance for faculty, curriculum developers, institutional administration, industry partners, and accrediting or policy bodies involved in curriculum and assessment framework design. Further, the findings may inform the rationale for scaling EPA-based assessment frameworks to non-clinical educational contexts and offer recommendations to guide their adaptation, development, and implementation, addressing CBE assessment challenges and creating a replicable model for future non-clinical program development.
