abstract: Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii are fungal pathogens that cause life-threatening infections, including cryptococcal meningitis. A distinctive feature of the cryptococcal cell wall is the extensive deacetylation of chitin to chitosan, a modification that is essential for virulence but whose structural role in cell-wall organization remains poorly understood. Here, we analyze the cell walls of wild-type strains of both species and their avirulent chitosan-deficient mutants, which serve as vaccine candidates. Loss of chitosan disrupted cell morphology and altered cell-wall ultrastructure, with more pronounced defects in C. neoformans . Solid-state NMR reveals that aggregated α-(1→3)-glucans form the principal rigid domain of the cell wall in both species and are closely associated with chitin microfibrils, whereas surrounding β-glucans and mannoproteins constitute a more dynamic matrix. Chitosan modulates hydration and flexibility, and its loss increases chitin exposure and triggers species-specific remodeling of the polysaccharide network. In C. neoformans , chitosan depletion increased α-(1→3)-glucan content and reduced β-glucan levels, whereas C. gattii selectively lost one α-(1→3)-glucan subtype while maintaining β-glucan levels. Although capsule production remained intact, chitosan deficiency altered glucuronoxylomannan linkage patterns and mannoprotein composition. These findings reveal how chitosan organizes cryptococcal cell-wall architecture and highlight distinct structural adaptation strategies among pathogenic Cryptococcus species.

title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
abstract: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Code and website: https://github.com/pikulsomesh/developmental-world-models and https://pikulsomesh.github.io/developmental-world-models/

title: Label-Space Mismatch Distorts Cross-Cohort Evaluation in Breast Cancer Molecular Subtyping
abstract: Cross-cohort evaluation of breast cancer subtype classifiers is unreliable when source and target cohorts use different annotation standards: METABRIC labels six classes, PAM50 defines five, and a claudin-low prediction cannot be correct under a five-class standard. A classifier transferred from 1,369 METABRIC patients (train n=958) to TCGA-BRCA (n=987) and GSE21653 (n=266) separates three evaluation operations routinely conflated in cross-site comparisons. (1) Label-space restriction - an evaluation-rule change, not a retraining gain - is the dominant correction (73.76%->79.74% on TCGA-BRCA; 63.16%->68.42% on GSE21653); (2) EM prior correction on the reconciled space is an optional calibration step (Brier fidelity up, macro F1 down; to 80.65% and 74.06%); and (3) the target label space is not recoverable from unlabelled predictions (EM retains prior 0.0751 on the absent class; calibrated detectors fail), so compliance must come from cohort documentation. The protocol exposes why internal validation overstates cross-cohort value: multimodal fusion gains do not transfer (no configuration beats mRNA alone, n=694; McNemar p=0.13-1.00), and the genomic panel adds nothing to pathological complete response prediction over clinical variables (DeltaAUC = +0.0045). Clinically, without label-space compliance, cross-site accuracy comparisons misattribute annotation-standard differences to model skill; Luminal A/B and claudin-low boundary errors map to distinct treatment decisions; and subtype accuracy is a weaker portable endpoint than survival discrimination (external C-index 0.577-0.584). Reporting the cohort's allowed label set and applying label-space compliance are therefore prerequisites before any cross-cohort performance claim.

title: EEG Pathology Detection via Clinical Concept Bottleneck Models
abstract: Deep learning models for electroencephalography (EEG) pathology detection achieve competitive accuracy but offer limited interpretability. In this paper, we introduce concept bottleneck models (CBMs) for EEG pathology detection which use clinical EEG biomarkers computed analytically from the signal as a bottleneck to be used for prediction. Those concepts include band power, spectral ratios, alpha peak frequency and amplitude, hemispheric asymmetry and phase locking values. With the backbone based on shallow convolutional neural network (CNN), we compare a black box baseline with two variants of CBMs. The hybrid variant is a classifier receives a residual projection of the backbone features. The pure variant is a CBM where the classifier receives only the predicted concepts. Models are evaluated on abnormality detection and dementia classification followed by concept prediction quality and leakage analysis. Both CBMs approach the baseline on TUAB (82.7-82.9% vs 83.6%) and are 2-5 percentage points lower on CAUEEG (57.9-60.5% vs 62.7%). The pure CBM exhibits concept fidelity concern where the predicted concepts deviate from their ground truth values. Replacing them with their true values causes severe cost on accuracy by 26 and 22 points on TUAB and CAUEEG. The concept fidelity concern is mitigated by increasing the weight of the concept loss to match the ground truth concepts. the mitigation comes with small accuracy cost on TUAB but a relatively larger cost on CAUEEG. The code of the experiments and full logs are available at https://www.github.com/mhmdrdwn/cbm.

title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation
abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a non-uniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organisation of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome's topology, operationalised here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a new model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network - the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.
author_corresponding_institution: MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK

title: Distributed neural dynamics underlie the shift from movement preparation to execution
abstract: Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in non-human primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across the broader networks and support skilled memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography (MEG) during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that motor preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces - a separation that generalised across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatiotemporal transition across the brain: the state-shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 ms before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localised to the motor cortices alone.

title: Supramodal Coding of Detection and Confidence in the Human Cortex
abstract: Perception is inherently multisensory, yet it remains unclear whether the brain detects stimuli and evaluates confidence in these detections using circuits shared across senses or circuits specific to each modality. Prior evidence is limited: scalp electrophysiology cannot localize where a shared code operates, whereas functional imaging cannot resolve its timing. We recorded intracranial activity (stereoelectroencephalography) in eight patients with epilepsy who performed a near-threshold audiovisual detection task in which they reported, on each trial, whether a visual, auditory, or audiovisual stimulus was present and rated their confidence, both overall and separately for each modality. Analyzing high-gamma activity at the single-channel and region-of-interest levels, we found that stimulus detection involved a broadly distributed, largely supramodal set of cortical regions responding regardless of modality, including the insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and superior temporal gyrus. Multivariate decoders trained to distinguish detected from undetected stimuli in one modality generalized to the other modality, indicating a shared detection code within these regions. Confidence relied on a more mixed architecture but was also substantially supramodal. Finally, the auditory cortex encoded confidence information about its non-preferred (visual) modality, with a similar effect in the visual cortex for auditory confidence, suggesting that the involvement of sensory cortices in confidence is not confined to its preferred input.
author_corresponding_institution: Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Univ. Savoie Mont Blanc, CNRS, LPNC, 38000 Grenoble, France

title: Computational Evaluation of tDCS Montage Separability and Dose Coverage for Practice-Specific Mindfulness Experiments
abstract: A practice-specific stimulation experiment requires candidate montages that differ in regional electric-field exposure without sacrificing interpretable target dose. We evaluated this requirement for transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) montages intended to test focused-attention and open-monitoring mindfulness practices. Four focused-attention candidates and six open-monitoring candidates formed 24 pairs, evaluated with SimNIBS 4.6 in 20 existing anatomical head models at a linearly scaled current of 2 mA. Outcomes were regional 99th-percentile field magnitude, a normalized double-dissociation index (DDI), suprathreshold overlap, and individual dose coverage. Eighteen pairs passed four recorded progression criteria, but only five also met a post hoc requirement that both intended regional contrasts be positive in at least 80% of heads. A positive DDI alone concealed a reversed salience-region contrast in one conventional comparison. The nominated F3-centered 4-by-1 ring paired with F8-Fp2 sponges (FA-05 x OM-02) produced both directional preferences in 20/20 heads, with median DDI 1.561 and median suprathreshold Dice 0.000. The conventional F3-Fp2 and FT8-FCz sponge pair (FA-02 x OM-07) produced both preferences in 19/20 heads, with DDI 0.627 and Dice 0.186. Both anatomical targets reached the operational 0.20 V/m floor in 11/20 versus 20/20 heads, respectively. ROAST 4.0, with ring placement held fixed, supported both nominations but exposed dose disagreement. Across conductivity sensitivity draws, directional separability persisted more consistently than absolute dose. These results establish a regional separability-dose trade-off within the tested candidate set and show why a summed contrast cannot substitute for a directional conjunction. They support selection of a discriminating experiment, not whole-network selectivity, physiological efficacy, or a validated treatment.

title: Kilohertz electrical stimulation drives widespread neuronal activation and temporal interference imposes focal rhythmic modulation
abstract: Temporal interference (TI) stimulation has attracted attention as a non-invasive approach that can target deep brain structures through interacting kilohertz-frequency electric fields. Its basic premise is that TI stimulation evokes neuronal responses through low-frequency amplitude modulation (AM), while the underlying kilohertz-frequency stimulation is ineffective to induce activity, the latter of which has not been tested rigorously at the cellular level. Here, we combined two-photon imaging in mouse models with immunohistochemistry and computational modeling to characterize spatiotemporal patterns of neuronal responses during TI stimulation. We found that kilohertz-frequency stimulation was sufficient to evoke activity without AM. In contrast, AM organized neuronal activity into rhythmic responses at AM frequency, with the strongest entrainment near the center of interference. Thus, kilohertz-frequency stimulation can drive widespread neuronal activation, upon which TI imposes focal rhythmic modulation. Our results provide a framework for refining TI stimulation and highlight the potential of kilohertz-frequency stimulation for brain stimulation.

title: Striatal D2-neurons gate D1-mediated associative encoding under uncertainty
abstract: Goal-directed actions are established through the encoding of predictive relationships between behaviour and its consequences, a process involving dopamine-dependent plasticity in the dorsal striatum. Early phases of learning entail complex associative landscapes from which useful action-outcome contingencies must be identified. Although dopamine processes are central to associative learning, the cellular mechanisms through which behaviourally relevant plasticity is selected from competing signalling events remain unknown. Here we show that D2-spiny projection neurons (D2-SPNs) are transiently recruited during the earliest stages of instrumental learning, when critical action-outcome contingencies emerge. We identify a dominant cell-to-cell transmodulation process by which D2-SPNs regulate dopamine-dependent signalling by constraining protein kinase A activity in D1-SPNs. This mechanism overrides extracellular dopamine signals and can be reproduced in vivo through calibrated optogenetic activation of cAMP signalling. Enhancing D2[->]D1-SPN transmodulation during uncertain reinforcement schedules durably improves action-outcome encoding, revealing a mechanism through which striatal networks promote relevant contingencies under associative ambiguity.

title: Validation of a Commercially Available Non-Woven Fabric Electrode for Mouse Electroretinography
abstract: Purpose: To evaluate the performance and usability of a commercially available nonwoven fabric electrode as a cost-effective and user-friendly alternative to standard corneal contact lens electrodes for recording murine electroretinography (ERG). Methods: Full-field ERGs were recorded in the same individual mice using both the commercially available non-woven fabric electrode and a conventional contact lens electrode in a paired design. Key parameters evaluated included (1) baseline noise stability, (2) dark-adapted intensity-response curves (0.01-100 cd{middle dot}s{middle dot}m-2), (3) light-adapted intensity-response curves (3-100 cd{middle dot}s{middle dot}m-2), (4) 20 and 30 Hz flicker responses, (5) extended recordings targeting slow c-wave kinetics under dark-adapted conditions, and (6) inter-eye consistency via bilateral simultaneous recordings. Results: Eliminating the need for viscous lubricants, the non-woven fabric electrode simplified corneal placement, alignment, and re-application. It yielded a- and b-wave amplitudes and peak times comparable to those obtained with standard contact lens electrodes. Notably, during prolonged recordings, the non-woven fabric electrode yielded significantly larger c-wave amplitudes while maintaining equivalent baseline noise stability. Bilateral simultaneous recordings demonstrated high inter-eye correlation and low measurement variability between contralateral eyes. Conclusions: The non-woven fabric electrode provides high-quality, reproducible ERG recordings comparable to, and for c-waves superior to, standard corneal contact lens electrodes. This accessible method facilitates standardized data acquisition and enhances inter-laboratory reproducibility in murine ERG. Translational Relevance: By reducing financial and technical barriers, this non-woven fabric electrode offers an alternative to specialized recording setups, improving experimental throughput and efficiency in ophthalmic research.
